title: Game Design: Systems, Mechanics, and Player Experience
description: A course for learners who have played games critically and perhaps made small prototypes, and now want the working methods of professional designers. It treats a game as a system of rules that produces player experience, and teaches the tools designers use to shape that system: core loops, feedback, economies, difficulty curves, level layout and playtesting. Every chapter ends with a design exercise that you can complete on paper or in a simple prototype.
prerequisites: Regular, attentive experience playing games in several genres
Basic arithmetic and spreadsheets; no programming required
objectives: Analyze a game in terms of mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics.
Design and diagram a core loop and its feedback systems.
Balance a small game economy using a spreadsheet model.
Plan a difficulty and pacing curve and lay out a level that teaches through play.
Run a playtest, collect usable evidence and turn it into design changes.
Write a concise design document for an original game concept.

preface:
This book is for people who have played a lot of games, maybe built a prototype or two, and now want to work the way designers in studios work. Each chapter gives you one set of tools, shows it at work in games you probably know (*Tetris*, *Super Mario Bros.*, *Slay the Spire*), and then asks you to use it on a design of your own.

That design is a small card game you start in Chapter 1 and improve in every chapter after it. Paper, index cards and a spreadsheet are all you need. Paper is faster than code for learning design, because you can change a rule in ten seconds and play again.

Expect your first versions to be bad; everyone's are. The real skill this book teaches is noticing why a design is not working and changing it, which is why playtesting runs through every chapter and gets one of its own.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a working game designer would: from shipped games, playtests, prototypes and spreadsheets.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to take a game apart, say why it works, and design, test and improve one of your own.
threads: A game is a system of rules that produces player experience (mechanics to dynamics to aesthetics).
Prototype on paper and playtest early: evidence beats opinion.
Every concept is shown in real, well-known games, then applied to your own design.

conventions: Italicize game titles and give the release year at first mention.
Use MDA terms consistently: mechanics, dynamics, aesthetics.
Every chapter ends with a concrete step on the reader's pocket card game.
